questions.question: In the MCPA Security and Governance domain, what does auditability add beyond real-time observability?
options: It replaces real-time monitoring entirely, since a stored log shows everything a live dashboard already shows
It lets a reviewer reconstruct and verify what happened after the fact, using durable recorded evidence
It measures how quickly a tool call finishes, which a monitoring dashboard is not able to measure
It stores a full copy of the model's weights, so training can be repeated exactly step by step
questions.explanation: Observability is real-time visibility into current behavior, while auditability is the ability to reconstruct and independently verify past behavior from durable, tamper-evident records after an incident.

questions.question: Why does altering a past entry in a hash-chained audit log get detected when the chain is verified?
options: Each entry is individually encrypted with a private signing key, so only the person holding that key can open it
Each entry is copied out to three separate backup servers, so a majority vote decides which stored copy is authentic
Each entry is also stamped by an external clock service, so any later secret edit would simply show the wrong date
Each entry's hash covers the previous hash plus its own content, so editing a past entry breaks its recorded hash value
questions.explanation: A hash chain ties each entry to the one before it through the hash value itself, so changing any past entry's content produces a different hash than the one recorded, and the mismatch is detectable.

questions.question: Why must a flagged sensitive field be redacted before an audit entry is written and hashed, rather than only masked later when the log is displayed?
options: Because the durable record must never contain the secret, or anyone reading the stored log or its backups can recover it later
Because redacting an entry only after it has already been written would make that one particular tool call run measurably slower every time
Because a display-time mask would silently change the tool's name, which would break the audit log's hash chain
Because the protocol specification requires every request to be encrypted twice before any server is allowed to execute it
questions.explanation: Redaction has to happen before an entry is created, because a durable or backed-up log that ever stored the raw secret has already leaked it, no matter how a later viewer displays that entry.

questions.question: How does an allowlist that denies an unregistered tool differ from what the audit log itself does?
options: The allowlist only applies to tools that are written in Python, while the audit log applies to tools written in any language
The allowlist is optional and can be skipped by the model, while the audit log is mandatory for every request
The allowlist stops a call before it runs at all, while the log only records calls that were allowed to execute
The allowlist encrypts every argument before a call runs, while the audit log decrypts those arguments for a human reviewer
questions.explanation: An allowlist is a risk control that prevents a disallowed tool from ever executing, while the audit log is a record of what already happened, so the two serve different points in the same request's lifecycle.

questions.question: An attacker with write access to the log file edits a past entry's arguments and also recomputes that one entry's own stored hash to match the new content. What happens when verify() runs next?
options: Verification passes cleanly, because a hash chain can only detect a change to the single most recent entry in the log
The edited entry's own hash matches again, but the next entry's stored previous-hash no longer matches it, so verification still catches the break
Verification fails immediately on the first entry in the log, regardless of which later entry the attacker actually changed
Verification is skipped entirely, because recomputing just one entry's hash disables the chain check for every single entry after it in the log
questions.explanation: A hash chain protects against exactly this move: repairing one entry's own hash does not repair the link the following entry holds back to it, so the break is still visible at that later point.

questions.question: A support tool resets a user's password. The team wants proof the reset happened without the new password ever sitting in the audit log. Which control accomplishes this?
options: Raising the per-tool rate limit, so the password-reset tool is allowed to run as many times as the entire support team needs it to
Adding the password tool to the allowlist, so the server will accept a request to run it at all
Increasing the required arguments on the schema, so the caller must supply more fields before the tool can run
Marking the password argument as a flagged field, so it is replaced with a fixed marker before the entry is written or hashed
questions.explanation: Redaction targets the one field that must never be stored, replacing it with a fixed marker before the entry exists in any form, which is a different job than deciding whether the tool may run or how often.
